title: Trash by James Caverly and Andrew Morrill at the Perelman Arts Center...
transcript: A sex banshee, an ankle monitor, and a secret love affair are just some of the points of conflict in this new play called Trash. Although roommates Jake and Tim have a somewhat contentious relationship, a dispute over who should take out the trash only skimming the surface, both of them benefit from living with a fellow deaf person. The play is performed in ASL with occasional subtitles and dubbing, and the actors sometimes use whiteboards to communicate with each other and the audience. There's an element of audience participation where everyone is given a double sided piece of cardboard that they vote with throughout the play. These factors keep the show engaging and accessible for everyone. That said, I appreciate how the piece doesn't overly cater itself toward hearing people, as there’s not voicing the entire time — you're sometimes just picking up what you can from visual cues, which is quite a lot with such strong performances from the entire cast. While the show takes place exclusively in Jake and Tim's apartment, it covers a lot of ground — discrimination and marginalization, assimilation, appropriation, and relationship dynamics between deaf and hearing people are just some of the topics this play explores. Although some of the discussions of deaf culture feel a little unrealistically direct within the context of this story, it provides a window for everyone including hearing audience members to understand these characters more deeply. It's not a perfect play — a little unfocused and overblown, but I thought it was really well done, with great performances and direction. And, it was of course a privilege to get a glimpse into deaf culture in such a captivating way. Trash is running at the Perelman Arts Center through March 28th. With that, another program for my collection.
